Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I apologize for not sending him notice, but this news came to our attention only a short time ago.
Has the minister any information to give the house with respect to the reported death of Patrice Lumumba of the Congo? Has the government given consideration to what contribution we will make to meet the situation that will flow from this unfortunate incident?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CONGO-REPORTED DEATH OF MR. LUMUMBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am aware of the radio report that Mr. Patrice Lumumba and two companions have been killed in circumstances which still remain to be clarified. If this report is accurate we deplore very much this act of violence. While Mr. Lumumba has been a controversial figure, the fact remains that he was a duly elected member of parliament and formed the first government of the newly independent republic of the Congo. His death, if it has taken place, is unlikely to settle anything. Indeed, it is more likely to complicate the already difficult task of the United Nations in the Congo and the process of conciliation and pacification which it is seeking to foster. For this reason and of course also, as I have mentioned, on humanitarian grounds the government is very much upset about this reported act of violence.
It is our hope that all parties will exercise restraint in this dangerous situation. As the hon. member knows, Canada is a member of the Congo committee at the United Nations, and throughout has tried to pour oil on troubled waters. We will continue to follow that course if this death has actually taken place.
I believe that the Secretary General of the United Nations asked today for instructions to make an investigation. That request was supported, for example, by the representative of the United States, and an investigation is now under way. The security council will be meeting on the question, I think, on Wednesday.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chown (for Mr. Woolliams) for the second reading of Bill No. S-2, to incorporate Aurora Pipe Line Company, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Peters.

maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to inform the house that the members of our group will oppose the bill now under discussion. We think a mistake has been made in asking the house to give second reading to the Aurora pipe line bill.
It has been said that what the house is being asked to do today is to give routine approval to a bill that will subsequently go before a committee of this house, and that after the company is incorporated it will then have to get approval from the national energy board before it can in fact export gas, oil or condensates to the United States. While this statement is true, Mr. Speaker, the responsibility of this house to deal with this question cannot be handed over quite so easily to a committee of the house or to a board.
It has been already pointed out on a number of occasions in this debate that a bill passed by this house established a Canadian company which has power to provide a pipe line for the exportation to the United States of products which are covered by the bill under discussion.
Our main objection to the bill now before the house, Mr. Speaker, is based on the very ground that the Conservative party and the C.C.F. took in this house in 1956 during the

pipe line debate, in opposition to the trans-Canada pipe line bill. The bill before us provides for the incorporation of another company that will be under United States control. About two thirds of the shares of the company will be controlled by a United States company, the Continental Oil Company. This is another instance of a great natural resource being controlled in its transportation by a United States company.
We think there are on record, on previous occasions, adequate reasons why this bill should be opposed. The Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, and other members of the house on a former occasion objected to the Texas buccaneers having a large part of the control of the trans-Canada pipe line company. The Texas buccaneers are involved in this measure. There has been in my judgment, a complete reversal of the stand that was taken by the Conservative party in 1956. By supporting this bill hon. members will turn the ownership, and control of this pipe line over to a United States company. Back in 1956, on June 4, the leader of the opposition at that time, Hon. George Drew, put forward a very important proposition by way of an amendment to the trans-Canada pipe line bill then before the house. I should like to read, if I may, the provisions of that amendment, because I think they might be made applicable at this time to this bill. The amendment is found on page 4673 of Hansard for that date, and reads as follows:
That the bill be not now read the third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions that they have the power to amend sections 5, 6 and 7 thereof to include the agreements made with Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited as schedules to the bill and add other sections necessary to ensure that the bill shall give effect to one of the following principles.
First, the immediate agreement of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited to reorganize as a company under effective Canadian ownership and control and to undertake construction without a grant of public money, in accordance with the assurances upon which its charter was granted by parliament;
The proposition was that the trans-Canada pipe line company should be reorganized under Canadian control.
Second, failing such agreement, the immediate consideration of other proposals submitted by any other persons or companies for the immediate financing and construction of the pipe line under effective Canadian ownership and control and without a grant of public money;
There is a company already in existence that can do this work and I suggest that this United States proposal to which we are being asked to agree at this time should be opposed by the members of the house, and this bill should be defeated.
Third, enlarge the powers of the crown corporation so that the entire pipe line may be constructed immediately under public ownership.

The Conservatives of that day, Mr. Speaker, went so far as to say that if the government refused to accept the first two propositions then, as a third alternative, the pipe line should be publicly owned. The bill we are being asked to pass today repudiates the whole policy and position taken by the Conservative party in those days. It makes a mockery-

speechtext:
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I feel that the present speaker is not confining himself to the principle involved in this bill, according to the ruling you made as recorded on page 1818 of Hansard. You said:
As I see it, the principle of the bill is whether this group of individuals petitioning parliament shall be given corporate capacity. I see no principle other than this involved in this bill, whether this particular group of individuals shall be given corporate capacity.
I would ask you, sir, to enforce that ruling.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext: The remarks, as I followed them, did not seem to me to call for intervention. maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question before he continues? He said earlier in the debate, with some authority, that the shares would be two thirds United States owned. I was going to ask him how he could make that suggestion to the house in the light of the fact that section 3, (a) and (b), simply provides for share capital. No one in this chamber can presume what the apportionment of ownership will be as between the United States and Canada, or as between any particular groups of individuals no matter where they reside.

maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext:
This is a very interesting observation from the hon. member. I think it can only mean one thing, that he is challenging what I have said as not being a statement of fact. It will be very interesting to see, if this motion should pass and the bill come out of the committee, that we have been wrong and this is a Canadian company. I hope I am in error, but I am afraid I am not.
One of my reasons for thinking I am not in error is that the gentleman who introduced this bill in the other place, when explaining it said that the company was

owned one third by the Hudson's Bay Company and two thirds by the Continental Oil Company, the latter being one of the large integrated oil companies in the United States. I am prepared to accept the word of the hon. senator. I hope he is in error. I hope the hon. member for Winnipeg South, who has just asked the question, is right. maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext: May I raise a point of order? I think those words used by the hon. member for Assiniboia run counter to citations 482 and 483 of Beauchesne, to the effect that the facts cannot be questioned in the house during the debate on a private bill. These are matters for the committee. There is no question that the facts cannot be discussed during the discussion on second reading.

maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext: I should like to speak to that point of order, Mr. Speaker, if I may. In support of the argument, and even going beyond the authority cited by my colleague, I would say that at the time the earlier debate on the pipe line took place the National Energy Act, which is chapter 46 of the statutes of 1959, had not been enacted. If you refer to section 44 of that act, Mr. Speaker, you will find that when a company makes an application to export gas, even if they are incorporated by a bill they have to be certified by the national energy board. This is the point of order-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext: If the hon. member is coming to the point of order I would be glad to have his assistance. It seems to me he is answering the argument of the hon. member who had the floor.

maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext: I am coming to the point of order. I think the hon. member is confined more than he would have been in the previous debate because one of the circumstances to be taken into consideration by the energy board is the very fact to which the hon. member has referred. We have this legislation on the books, and that goes beyond the principle of the bill. All we are asking here is the incorporation of a legal entity, not for permission to construct a pipe line or export anything through the pipe line; merely the right to be incorporated. The other right is a right for a court of record, namely the national energy board, to decide when circumstances are set out by evidence, and they make that decision. That is my point.

speechtext: You just want to sell the country to the Americans.

speechtext: I wonder whether I might be allowed to say a word on the point of order that has been raised. Do I understand hon. gentlemen opposite to be seeking to restrict debate in this chamber on a pipe line?

maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext: A point of order has been raised as to whether hon. members may discuss the ownership of the proposed pipe line on second reading, since the national energy board has power, according to section 44 of the act, to take into account the extent to which the Canadians will have the opportunity to participate in the financing. I would point out that in the National Energy Board Act there is no provision which requires Canadian ownership of a pipe line of this description. It is obvious that this pipe line is not to be Canadian owned. For that reason I am expressing opposition to the passage of the bill.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext:
Order. The parliamentary secretary has raised a point of order which draws a distinction between the scope of debate on a public bill and that on a private bill. I think I might read citation 482 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, to which I am referred:
A public bill being founded on reasons of state policy, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, accepts and affirms those reasons; but the expediency of a private bill, being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill, conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee. Where, irrespective of such facts, the principle is objectionable, the house will not consent to the second reading; but otherwise, the expediency of the measure is usually left for the consideration of the committee. This is the first occasion on which the bill is before the house otherwise than pro forma or in connection with the standing orders; and if the bill be opposed, upon its principle, it is the proper time for attempting its defeat.
Citation 483 is to somewhat the same effect. Undoubtedly there is a narrower margin for debate on a private bill than on a public bill. This is a private bill. At an earlier stage in this debate I endeavoured to prevent the house from embarking upon a general debate on the economics of the oil industry. However, it seems to me that it is relevant for an hon. member to express some views on the question of whether another pipe line company should be formed on such material as is before the house. It is true that the future and the intentions of this company are not relevant so much as the powers which it seeks to acquire. The powers are relevant because that is the principle of the bill; this particular group of petitioners have come before parliament asking to be given as a corporation the power to operate a pipe line company.

Private Bills
As certain tacts have been discussed in debate in this house and the hon. member has quoted from what has been said in debate-it is true in the other place-if he does not attempt to extend his allegation of facts to too great a degree, I think I should allow him to proceed.

maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The house is being asked to give second reading to this bill, which is approval in principle. It is perfectly true that it is a conditional type of approval, in that the bill will be placed before a committee of this house for detailed examination. The bill might be killed in the committee; it might be referred back to the house in a different form.
Mr. Speaker, what we are objecting to is any kind of approval of this bill, whether conditional or unconditional. We think it is a thoroughly bad bill. We think the people of Canada in the past, when they have had a chance to make a judgment, have shown that they favour Canadian development of gas pipe lines in this country. The Conservative government is in power today in this country to a substantial degree because of the public support that was given to the opposition parties of the day in opposing pipe lines in this country being owned and controlled by outside capital. Today I am opposing this bill, as is the C.C.F.-New party, because we think it is a thoroughly bad bill, an un-Canadian bill, and one that goes counter to the public statements of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance made on many occasions. We think the passage of this bill to set up another United States company is not in the interests of Canadians at this time. For the life of me I cannot understand why there appears to be-and only a vote on this matter will show whether or not I am correct-such general and widespread approval of United States buccaneers owning this pipe line in opposition to the stand taken by Conservative members of parliament in this House of Commons on so many occasions.

speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question.

maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS

speechtext:
The hon. member for Bow River can make his own speech. He will have an opportunity to show how much he loves the Texas buccaneers. The Tories did not formerly love them, as you know, Mr. Speaker, but they have changed. Since the Tories got into office the Texas buccaneers became fine fellows. The Tories are for them now. Even though a Canadian company could do the job, they are rising in their places in a unified chorus today giving their "Amen" to a bill which will turn a pipe line over to United States control.

Mr. Speaker, we are asked by means of a private bill to endorse in principle the organization of another pipe line. As we understand it, this pipe line is going to be largely owned outside of Canada, and if permitted to be built the operation of this pipe line will injure the interests of an existing pipe line that has already been authorized to do this work by a previous parliament.
I find it difficult to understand why hon. members would endorse the principle of inviting a foreign owned pipe line into Canada in order to ruin a bona fide Canadian company. I also have difficulty understanding why a private bill should become a matter of party politics. I do not see that the life of the government is involved in this bill. There is a growing tendency in Canada to make even private legislation a matter of party politics. I regret that development. The government's life is not involved here. This is not a government sponsored bill. I cannot understand why political parties have to take party line positions with respect to private bills, and I deplore this development.
Legislation offered to us by the government, if it is not of major significance, ought not to be subject to the whips of the parties. This is not a new tendency but it is a growing one. Party lines are the determining factor with respect to legislation even including private bills. I conclude my remarks with this observation. I believe that political parties ought to be cut down to size and members of parliament restored to their proper status so they can make up their own minds whether this bill and others of a similar nature are in the interests of the nation rather than of the political parties.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to support my own bill I would first like to thank the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Chown) for his assistance during the time I was unavoidably absent from the house.
I should like to deal first with the references to the principle of the bill which we are debating. The petitioners, the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited, are simply asking for the incorporation of a federal company. They are not asking for the right to build a pipe line; they are not asking for the right to export any commodity through a pipe line; they are merely asking this House of Commons for a certificate of incorporation to incorporate a company. I think that is the first principle we should consider in reference to this bill.
It may be of some interest to look at the record for a few moments in reference to the bill itself. I am going to review this matter very briefly. The petitioners are the two vice presidents, and council as 1 just said, of the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company. Approximately 10 per cent of the shares of the company is held by 12,000 public shareholders; 22 per cent is held by the Hudson's Bay company; and 68 per cent is held by the Continental Oil Company.
Let us take a look first of all at the 10 per cent that is held by the public shareholders. I am not sure who those shareholders are, or will be, but there are some Canadian investors. Twenty two per cent is owned by the Hudson's Bay Company which, of course, as everyone knows, received a charter to operate its business in Canada by royal declaration. I would say it is wholly a Canadian company. The Continental Oil Company have 68 per cent of the stock. This is how the shares are distributed.
The company is interested in this project and it is designed to assist in the solution of a problem which has arisen in that part of Alberta which is the Pincher Creek area, the southern part. In the process of making natural gas there are different by-products and condensates produced. Let us put it in ordinary layman's language. Condensate is similar to crude oil, the only difference being that you can make one and one half times more gasoline from condensates.

In answer to some of the arguments in the debate, there have been discussions with reference to the obtaining of a market for petroleum in the province of Alberta. Since I come from the province of Alberta I should like to see an enlarged market. I am one who wants to see condensate exported, and the cheapest and the only way in which it can be exported from the fields in Alberta is of course, by pipe line.
Therefore when we start talking about byproducts we are talking about something the average man uses. It is gasoline for his automobile; that is the by-products. It is interesting to note also that if this company is able to sell, transport and export those by-products from the province of Alberta, then the consumer of natural gas would get a reduction in rates and would thereby make a saving.
I should like now to refer to this red herring, as I call it, which relates to our position in so far as United States capital and United States companies operating in Canada are concerned. My answer to that is briefly this. I have never considered any words used by any members of the cabinet or any members of the government as being against capital coming from anywhere, whether it was from the United States or any country in Europe. The only thing for which this government has stood, and I am proud to be a Conservative in that regard, is that Canadians can compete on equal terms with capital coming into this country from other sources. There have been times in the history of this country, such as 1915 and the boom in the 1920's and the 1950's, during which United States capital and capital from other countries was needed in order to develop the resources of this country. I say that is a red herring when they talk about turning our industry over to the buccaneers.
The truth is that the buccaneers of the province of Saskatchewan, the socialist government, chased capital out of that province so that now they have not industry comparable to that of the province of Alberta. The truth is that the budget of the province of Alberta is three or four times greater than that of the province of Saskatchewan because we have encouraged capital, not only Canadian but other capital, to pour into that province and develop our resources so that Canadians in that province will have employment. Those people over in that corner are always talking about unemployment. I am one of those who believe that if we can develop our industry, then one of the first things to do is incorporate a company for a purpose. Once that company is incorporated for a purpose it gets into business and, with the proper flow of capital, provides jobs for 90205-6-125

I should like to answer two or three remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver East. As I said the other day, there is one thing that differentiates the hon. member from the other seven in that group. Even though I disagree with him, he always has something to say. He did say this, as recorded on page 1129 of Hansard for January 17, 1961:
-I simply cannot understand how a Tory could sponsor this bill when one calls to mind the principles expounded with such verbosity by the Minister ol Finance (Mr. Fleming) in his baby budget relating to Canadian control and Canadian development of Canadian companies.

I am not one who always goes along with everything that someone else may suggest, whether it comes from the front benches or some of the back benches. I say that any political party will be healthy, Mr. Speaker, if it has men such as we have in our party who are independent thinkers. They can consider a problem and arrive at a compromise. I moved this bill as a private member, and it has nothing to do with the government. I moved it as a private member because I believe in the economic welfare of my province.
If we have this company incorporated, then it will have the right to go to the energy board. Let us look at that argument for a few minutes. If I followed the argument of hon. gentlemen correctly, and it is sometimes difficult to follow them, they were opposed to this bill because 68 per cent of the stock of the petitioner is owned by a company in which the majority shareholders are from the United States. These gentlemen believe, therefore, that these petitioners should not be granted the right to incorporate a company because there might be United States capital used.

There may be other pipe line companies in Alberta that have the same interests as this company seeking incorporation through this bill. Other companies, already incorporated, can go before the national energy board. If this house does

The applicant must receive the right to export a commodity through a pipe line. This company or the Foothills Pipe Line Company or any other company that is incorporated which desires to export condensates or any other by-product must get a certificate from the board.
Let us analyse section 44. When the government introduced the bill to establish the national energy board, all these points that have been raised by my good friends in the corner must be considered by the board. This is now a question of law. Let us look at some of these things this court of record will consider. They will consider, first, the availability of oil or gas to the pipe line or power to the international power line; second, the

existence of markets, actual or potential; third, the economic feasibility of the pipe line or international power line; fourth, the financial responsibility and the financial structure of the applicant, the method of financing the line and the extent to which Canadians will have an opportunity to participate in the financing, engineering and construction of the line.
When these people in the corner refer to this party as supporting United States buccaneers, Mr. Speaker, I do not know what they mean by that statement. This is one of the things spelled out in the National Energy Board Act by this government and by this party in order to protect Canadian interests, to ensure that Canadian interests have a fair shake with any other financial interests in this land of ours in the development of our resources, whether it be petroleum, natural gas or any other resource.
This board is made up of reliable personnel. Before they would consider an application by this company in question they would take into consideration all the factors set out in section 44 of the said act.
I therefore, say, Mr. Speaker, that all this talk by the C.C.F. in this debate about handing over our resources to the Americans or to anyone else is plain hogwash. The fact is that the national energy board was set up by this party and by this government for the sole purpose of protecting Canadians in Canada operating in competition with United States capital or with capital coming in from anywhere else. Surely that is fair and square treatment. That is why many hon. members in this house rose on points of order in order to state that all we are asking for is merely the right to incorporate a company which will go before a board governed by certain principles of law and brought into being by this party for the protection of Canadians, in order to obtain that certificate. The function of the energy board is to determine who shall build pipe lines and who shall export products.
We might go back for a moment to the question of the debate on the national energy board. I should like to read from my own remarks in that regard as follows, as reported at page 3980 of Hansard of May 25, 1959:
In brief, I commend this legislation to hon. members because the authority to permit the building of a pipe line and the obtaining of an export licence are under the jurisdiction of one body, the energy board.
As found at page 3981 of Hansard of 1959 I pointed out that was the very reason the board was set up, and provision was made for flexibility. The right to build a pipe line and the right to export whatever it is you are going to export through the pipe line can be determined by the board expeditiously by using the same evidence and the same records,

something which makes this board, as I have said before, a court of record. Therefore to these people who have been critical in reference to this matter I say that this is no move on my part personally or on the part of anyone who may have supported me in this regard. We are merely asking-and I am going to repeat the request-for the right to incorporate a company.
I often wonder what might happen in this country in the future if men like those seven or eight in the corner had an opportunity to form a government and keep out capital that developed the resources of this country in order to give Canadians jobs. Those people merely give lip service to principles. They live in the hope that there might be a recession or depression in this country so they can say, "Here we have unemployment; you people are to blame".

PROPOSED EXEMPTION FOR COSTS OF TUITION, BOOKS, ETC.
speechtext: That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act so as to provide for the exemption from income taxes of tuition fees paid to universities, vocational training schools, military colleges, academies and other institutions of higher learning, as well as the costs of all textbooks and scientific equipment necessary to the courses followed in these institutions of learning.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED EXEMPTION FOR COSTS OF TUITION, BOOKS, ETC.
speechtext: Before the hon. member begins, I wonder whether he would agree with me that to some extent his motion is anticipated by the budget resolution which now stands before the committee of ways and means and which covers tuition fees. That, of course, does not apply to the remainder of the hon. member's motion, but to that extent the debate would be somewhat curtailed.

maintopic: PROPOSED EXEMPTION FOR COSTS OF TUITION, BOOKS, ETC.
speechtext:
If I may I should like to point out at the outset that in my humble opinion they are altogether different motions. It is true that in the course of the discussion the question of university fees or higher education may come up, but the objectives these motions seek are as far apart as could be imagined.
I respectfully point out at once in what way I think they are so vastly different, and I should like to do this at the outset in order to emphasize that we are not covering the same ground. I find, for example, that the resolution which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has on the order paper refers to an exemption for students only; exclusively those students who are attending a university, and those students who are making income tax returns. My resolution suggests income tax relief for anyone who pays income tax; it might be, for instance, a father, or it might be an uncle who wishes to educate a nephew, or a niece.
There is a second difference which is basic. The minister's resolution exempts the fees only. My resolution seeks an exemption in respect of the cost of textbooks and scientific instruments and equipment used in scientific institutions. Take, for example, students of medicine who must use microscopes. These instruments can be very costly indeed. I am asking for exemption in this sphere, too.
There is a third difference which is also very important. The minister's resolution refers to full time students only, meaning students who are attending universities all day and taking a full course. My resolution goes beyond that. It calls for an exemption in respect of fees paid by everyone including students who are following courses in the
[Mr. Woolliams.i
evening, those who have to work during the day and who are attempting to improve their education. These are the people who really need such assistance as I am proposing. My resolution also refers to part-time students, not necessarily to students who are taking the full course.
Then again, the minister's resolution refers to exemptions only in respect of courses leading to a degree. Now there are schools of higher education whose courses do not always lead to a degree. For example, a student might be taking a post-graduate course in languages, without aspiring to a degree; or he might be taking a partial course in one branch of higher education or another which would not lead to a degree. Again, he might be attending a conservatory of music, which does not confer degrees.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman who raised this question is familiar with the fact that there is some difficulty connected with private members' resolutions finding their way and being reached on the order paper. Rarely are they reached on the order paper in the same session in which they are submitted. When the time comes close for them to be discussed they are chosen by some form of rotation or lot. Consequently there is no opportunity for an hon. member to

have his resolution proceeded with until a lapse of some time has transpired even though he conceived the proposal as many as five years before.
I do not propose to review the importance of higher education. It is important to the future of a progressive country. If I remember correctly, there was a private hon. member's bill debated in the last session which gave an opportunity for a full dress debate on the subject. At this point I should like to read into the record my resolution which is in the following words:
That, In the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act so as to provide for the exemption from income taxes of tuition fees paid to universities, vocational training schools, military colleges, academies and other institutions of higher learning, as well as the costs of all textbooks and scientific equipment necessary to the courses followed in these institutions of learning.
Under our constitution the field of education comes under the jurisdiction of provincial government. There has been a progressive and growing tendency in the last few years for the federal government to concern itself with the importance of higher education and an effort has been made to make higher education available to as many students as possible. Not long ago this house passed a measure providing assistance to universities. We as hon. members of this house should do what we can to make higher education available to as many as possible. One direct way of doing it would be to amend the Income Tax Act in the way envisaged in my resolution.
There are some countries-and one notable one-where students pay no fees for university education. That is an ideal situation in a country that is concerned with making education as widespread and readily available as possible. In other countries students fees are nominal. The fees students in Canada are called upon to pay are higher than those paid in most countries including the United States.
We are approaching a period-if it has not already arrived-where higher education is vital and where scientific training and training in various skills assume increasing importance. If we make prohibitive the cost of obtaining education in any of these fields we are not going as far as legislators should go in this area. We have the obligation as public men to make available to students increased opportunity of acquiring education. The steps represented by the resolution will be of some assistance in achieving this desirable end.
University education will certainly be available to many more young men and

Private Bills
women. As I said a moment ago, an education is no longer a luxury. It is a necessity. First of all, all parents are anxious to give their children an education, but a great many of them find it a struggle. We constantly hear stories, and facts have been presented to us, that children must be taken out of school. Promising and successful students must be taken out of college because their parents cannot afford to keep them there.
The adoption of this resolution would make it possible for relatives to assist in the education of children. An uncle or an aunt who may not be blessed with children of their own, may be in the position where they have a nephew or a niece whom they might wish to educate, and I am sure they would be prompted to do this if they could get exemption from income tax on the amount spent to educate students. Then, too, large corporations or employers of labour would arrange to see that promising children would be able to go to university. Certainly, those organizations will help to pay school fees if they know that they will be exempt from income tax on the amount spent in that way.
I do not wish to belabour this point very much. I know that people all across the country are concerned with the possibility of getting relief by way of income tax on the amounts paid in school fees, and so forth. It might be of interest to refer to some correspondence which I have received. I will read a letter from the students administrative council of the University of Toronto:
Dear Mr. Crestohl:
I am directed by the students' administrative council to advise you that the council, representing the undergraduates of the University of Toronto, supports wholeheartedly the private bill which they understand you intend to introduce in the House of Commons. We understand this bill suggests the government consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act in order to provide exemption from income taxes of tuition fees paid to universities as well as the cost to students of all textbooks and scientific equipment necessary to the courses followed in these institutions of learning.

The date of the letter is February 10, 1954, just about the time that my resolution appeared for the first time. I have another letter from a civil servant in the city of Verdun, which reads as follows:
(Translation):
Dear Mr. Crestohl: I read with much interest the motion which is to be presented to the Ottawa legislature with regard to the exemption from

income taxes of tuition fees, etc. for young people who are studying at a university, technical school or the like.
The gesture will be much appreciated by salaried heads of families, like myself. I have three sons pursuing their higher education, which costs me something like $3,000 a year.
You can see what sacrifices we have to make.
It is a case of social justice, because I know of heads of families in my constituency who had to take their sons away from their studies for that reason.
(Text):
I have another letter from Mitchell, Ontario, which reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Crestohl:
You have my sincere thanks for taking up the matter of tax exemption in connection with university education costs.
I can give you a lead to some excellent material on the subject, a source which you may not know about. Less than a year ago the president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association in a T.V. address made the following statement. (My figures are approximately right) "In Britain the percentage of university students aided by bursaries is 70 per cent; in the United States the figure stands at 50 per cent; in Canada it stands at 14 per cent."
I am aware that you are not asking for more bursaries, but for some tax relief for people who are trying to finance students at university. May you keep up the fight. Thousands of parents will thank you or anybody who can achieve something. They will appreciate that your attitude is not the smug attitude of your opponent the finance minister.
He was not referring to the present Minister of Finance; he was referring to the minister of finance at the time, and I assume he could easily be referring to any finance minister who does not allow sufficient exemption from income tax. The next letter I have is from Lumsden, Saskatchewan, which reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Crestohl:
An item in the December 9th issue of the Leader-Post interested me. This item mentioned a resolution to be proposed by you calling for the exemption from income tax of tuition fees and expenses.
On behalf of my daughter and the many other young people, who first must earn the money to pay for further education of any kind, I hope this resolution will be favourably received and acted upon.
I have next a telegram from Toronto, which reads:
Strongly support your proposed motion to provide exemption from income taxes of university fees. Would be real help to many paying own way.
My next quotation is from Lestock, Saskatchewan. Although it is on a telegram form, I think it came through the mail. It reads:
Dear Mr. Crestohl:
Note by Canadian Press dispatch in the Winnipeg Tribune of the 9th December issue that you intend to bring into parliament resolution asking for exemption of certain higher education costs. I certainly hope that you are able to get this passed.

Certainly in Canada a higher education can be absolutely nothing but an asset to the country. I have a boy going through for a doctor, now in fourth year at university, and it is costing me roughly $1,600 a year to keep him there, which is a lot of money to take out of one's salary every year, plus income tax and 10 per cent pension fund for old age, which also helps keep one off the country's unemployment rolls. A child under the present system is unable to attend university or other school of higher learning and there must be a lot of children across Canada who are unable to go higher for financial reasons. I wish you Bvery success,
And so on. These letters and telegrams are an indication that the people across the country are seeking this relief. Those of us who have had children or have children at universities know how difficult it is to keep them there, and this is especially true of a man on a yearly salary. The parents have to work hard and make sacrifices; they have to forgo a great many things themselves in the hope of being able to educate their children. I think this gesture by the House of Commons of exempting the tuition fees paid by fathers and mothers would be most welcome, and I also think it is one that we should not hesitate to make.
I am concerned with the fact that while I believe every member of the House of Commons would support the principle of a resolution of this kind, yet the Minister of Finance -who refers to it in his budget and says that in principle it is the type of tax exemption that should be given-does not go far enough.
I believe the members of this house, if they had their choice, would support this resolution, not only with their speeches but with their vote. However, I am a little concerned that hon. members might be so enthusiastic about this thing that they will, to use an expression, kill it with kindness. I am afraid members will get up one after the other and support the motion, saying what a good thing it is but they will kill it with kindness by talking it out.
In closing my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to give a few very brief quotations from pedagogues. One says:
Education is a debt due from the present to future generations.
Let us as legislators, acknowledge that. The next one says:
Education is the cheapest defence of nations.
The third is:
Education is a better safeguard of liberty than a standing army. If we retrench the wages of the schoolmaster, we must raise those of the recruiting sergeant.
These are very forceful statements, and I commend their meaning to all the members of the house and ask that they be guided by them.

speechtext:
First of all, may I congratulate the hon. member upon his sincerity and determination over a long period of time in bringing this matter to the attention of the house. I am sure he will not mind if I poke a little fun at his theory, and the way in which it works. It seems to be that you do not get anywhere with the minister of finance in the House of Commons until you sit in opposition. If this theory were to be expanded to full flower it would mean there should be one minister of finance in the house and 264 people sitting in opposition giving him suggestions from one end of the day to the other about good measures for the well-being of the country. The fact is, as the hon. member has pointed out, he brought this matter before the house in 1954, perhaps in the same form, but the idea fell upon deaf ears.
Subsequently, as the result of the benevolent changes that were wrought in 1957, at least a part of his objective is being met. I think myself some of the credit for this should go to the people who came here in 1957 and 1958 with fresh ideas, some of which undoubtedly happened to coincide with those of the hon. member who has just taken his seat. There are good parts to this resolution, and also some poor parts, parts which contain dangers. I should like to mention those without, however, attempting to throw cold water on the idea the hon. member has put forward but rather with a view to pointing out the things which would have to be considered if the second part of his resolution were to be implemented.
First, I should like to say a word about the good things in the resolution. I think the idea of extending income tax exemptions to those who are not students, as we accept that term, is a good one. I presume the hon. member has in mind covering students who go to summer schools or night schools. I certainly commend this idea and I would wholeheartedly endorse it.
Then he put forward the idea that this type of income tax relief would provide an incentive to the people to sponsor students. This, again, is a good idea. This would expand our present notion of the parent being responsible for the education of his child and would include the family circle or even, as I understood the hon. member's remarks, people outside the family. I know there are many people who do make a point of assisting worthy young students at universities. This would be some recognition of what has been, up to now, a rather selfless attitude on their part.
No one would quarrel with that idea that we must get along with education as quickly as possible. The dramatic events over the

Private Bills
week end have shown the great lag in scientific achievement in our country as compared with another unfriendly economy. This would make anyone seize upon any possible alternative to meet such a challenge. These are the good points that I would wholeheartedly support.
It is the second half of the hon. member's resolution which gives the difficulty. Perhaps I could read it this way:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act so as to provide for the exemption from income taxes... of the costs of all text books and scientific equipment necessary to the courses followed in these institutions of learning.
This is the part that causes me to pause and consider. I believe this would give a wide open field for abuse unless the regulations were carefully drafted. In the first place, institutions of higher learning would be difficult to define. Then, too, the phrase "costs of all textbooks and scientific equipment necessary to the courses followed" is used. I do not know the hon. member's alma mater in law, although I realize he is one of the distinguished members of the Montreal bar. I pose this problem to the hon. member. As he knows, there are two main theories for the teaching of law. One is what we at Dalhousie University law school, the best one in Canada, call the case method. This method is used also by Harvard University. There is another approach to legal training which is known as the textbook method, which is more in line with the tradition of a liberal arts education.
I think that one could argue, under this resolution, that a law student who followed the case method would be entitled to deduct the expenses of buying the books in which these cases are to be found. As the hon. member realizes, there are thousands of such books, the Canadian reports, the British reports and the reports of the Canadian provinces. These are all the sources of material for the study of law by the case method. I use this merely as an illustration, Mr. Speaker, and I do not want to pursue it ad nauseam. It would appear to me that one could use the spirit of this resolution, if one were a gifted law student with a rather sharp eye for a technicality, to march forth from law school with one's law library completely assembled.
An engineering student, with a legal bent, could go forth from the engineering school with the equipment he needs for a professional practice already purchased, using the plea that this was scientific equipment necessary to his course. One could even go a step farther and imagine some graduate of the

Ontario agricultural college marching forth from that institution with harrows, plowshares, and harvesting machinery, again using the excuse that this was a part of the equipment necessary to study his course.
I realize that is stretching the point too far and that one could fairly well draw a line perhaps with regard to the agriculture graduate. But how do you draw the line in the first case I mentioned, namely that of the lawyer? After all, he is expected to read through thousands of cases in the three years of study and these thousands of cases are contained in thousands of law books. Or again, students of the liberal arts at the undergraduate level in the university may wish to buy one thousand great books or one hundred great books or ten thousand great books, to all of which he may refer during his education, on the plea that these books are necessary.
Admittedly the argument is disproportionate and one realizes that there is an absurdity somewhere. The difficulty is in ascertaining where common sense stops and absurdity begins. I say that in no niggling spirit against the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl). I think this particular point I have raised could be cured by some rather careful draftsmanship of the regulations involved. At least I have pointed out that there are problems in the carrying out of such a resolution. I think the Minister of Finance is to be commended for his budget approach and for solving the problem in a fairly workable manner. I hope the hon. member for Cartier will present his resolution again and again until most, if not all, of its spirit is met. I thoroughly enjoyed listening to his contribution to the debate as I am sure I shall enjoy the ones that will follow.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take part for a few minutes in this debate on this resolution this afternoon. I am particularly interested in the field of education as it affects those people who can least afford an education for their families. For this reason I should like to make one or two points this afternoon. First of all, I want to commend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for the steps he has taken with respect to the income tax laws as they affected university students prior to this year. I am sure the people of Canada generally have accepted the principle introduced in the budget for the solution of some of these problems.
I want to bring before the house a few specific cases I have in mind. One is that of an older couple who may have three or four growing children. There comes a time when these children have finished their public

schooling and have reached the age in life when they wish to attend university. Not too many years ago I was one of those who, after serving some time in the armed forces, was able to come out and take advantage of the veterans legislation with regard to education. This advantage, of course, is not available to our younger people. I am just wondering whether we could not have gone a little further with regard to the amount deductible from a student's earnings.
I have a letter from a young married man in the city of Edmonton. He tells me that while he was working at what he referred to as an ordinary job, although he was not able to get along too well on this basis, he decided that he would like to make an attempt at some other field of endeavour. He chose the field of accountancy. The necessity of his going back to school made it obligatory for his wife to go to work. She now has a job by means of which she is able to supplement the earnings sufficiently so that they are able to get along. Their baby sitter fees are something in the neighbourhood of $60 a month. I am wondering whether we could not have gone a little further and have included provision for deduction of these fees in our amendments to the Income Tax Act.
I am not too sure whether this resolution, as it reads, would be of a great deal of benefit, particularly to the students in the province of Alberta. I am aware of the fact that in some provinces a great deal of the cost of text books must be looked after by the students. In Alberta this is not entirely the situation. A great number of books are provided by the school boards. The important thing, therefore, is the amount of the tuition fees, a matter which is at present looked after in the amendments to the Income Tax Act.
In his remarks the minister stated that some students, in pursuing their university courses, earned sufficient money to incur income tax liability. He is proposing that a student in full-time attendance at a university, if he is proceeding toward a degree, be allowed to deduct the tuition fees he pays to the university when computing his taxable income. I am wondering whether we could not be a little more kind and make the total amount of the tuition fees and the total cost of the books involved in sending a student to school deductible in gross from the earnings of the married man in question. I only pass this thought on as a suggestion. This matter has been brought to my attention and I thought this was a good time to raise it.
I hope that the hon. member for Cartier will bring this bill before the house at another time so as to afford us the opportunity 90205-6-126

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to make a few comments on this resolution put forward by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl). In these days of keen competition in trade, in armaments and in ideologies we must not lose sight of the advantages of higher education extended to every individual in this country of ours.
This is a very interesting resolution. It proposes to encourage education by increasing the exemptions from income tax. I notice a tendency on the part of many people-not only the hon. member for Cartier-and many organizations to suggest adjustments in income tax every time they wish to encourage some socially desirable objective.
I would submit that a graduated income tax is the fairest of all methods of financing our government and furthermore of sharing some portion of our national income with those people who receive the least benefit from our national income. That being the case, I would suggest that all alternatives to reductions in income tax should be thoroughly scrutinized, examined and considered with a view to determining whether or not income tax should be reduced.
The present government have indicated great sympathy with the furtherance of higher learning in Canada. Since this government came into power in 1957 and accepted the responsibility of government they have encouraged higher learning in several important ways. First, may I say that they have increased the grants to universities from a basis of $1 per capita in the provinces to a basis of $1.50. That is an increase of 50 per cent and a very substantial increase in federal assistance to higher learning.
By legislation this year, through the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act, very substantial grants are being made to the provinces to assist higher education of all kinds. Also corporations have been encouraged to increase their contributions to universities through actions by this government.
In his budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) indicated his support of federal assistance to higher learning with these words which are to be found at page

Private Bills
1012 of Hansard for December 20, 1960. The Minister of Finance used these words when introducing the last budget:
Many deserving students require financial aid in order to attend university. Some provinces have inaugurated systems of loans to worthy students in need of direct financial assistance. These commendable plans are producing very beneficial results. The government is giving continuing study to this important aspect of the problem.
The other aspect concerns the Income tax position of students and those on whom they are dependent. I propose a measure of tax relief for university students and their parents.
Some students, while pursuing their university courses, earn sufficient money to incur an income tax liability. I am proposing that a student in full time attendance at a university, if he is proceeding toward a degree, be allowed to deduct the tuition fees he pays to the university when computing his taxable income.
The income tax law already provides special assistance to parents who are supporting children at university by allowing them to claim a deduction in respect of such children even after they have attained the age of twenty one years. However, if the student of any age has income in excess of $950 he ceases to qualify as a dependent, and his parent then forfeits the $500 exemption otherwise accorded to him by the law, even though he may be giving financial support to the student. I propose that the student's tuition fees be allowed as a deduction from his earnings in determining whether he qualifies as a dependent. If his income after deduction of his fees falls below $950 the parent will recover the $500 exemption.
These changes will become effective on January 1, 1961.
I have indicated that all alternatives should be examined before deciding to reduce income tax. I would like to refer to a suggestion brought forward by the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) who in her very fine speech in connection with the last budget debate made this suggestion, as reported at page 1355 of Hansard of January 24, 1961:
I should like to see federal loan banks for education available to all, young and old Canadians, not particularly based on need or the highest excellence in scholastic achievement, but on the prime requirement of a desire to learn. A revolving fund should be kept replenished by those who benefit most in this generation for those of the next generation, and we should be the first to recognize the enormous cost of university buildings, laboratories and libraries, and the competition for the best brains in the world, teachers and professors. It seems to me that if we have industrial loans, farm loans and loans for small business we should certainly have loans for the development of the brains-

Mr. Speaker, I shall observe your ruling, but I was trying to make the point that before deciding on such a method of assisting students as a reduction of income tax other alternatives should be reviewed. If that is out of order, I shall go on with one or two other observations.
The cost of education is ever on the increase. With our accumulation of knowledge increasing from generation to generation it becomes more difficult for each succeeding generation to master it, or at least it requires more time to impart that knowledge. Not only does it require more time on the part of the teachers, but it requires more time on the part of the students who are the recipients of that knowledge. Because more time is required the whole process of handing on this accumulated knowledge of the ages becomes more expensive. In making our national financial plan we should keep this fact in mind, and no doubt the hon. member for Cartier had that in mind when he made this proposal to encourage higher education by making certain reductions in income tax. I should like to speak briefly on this resolution this afternoon. First, I should like to compliment the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) on having brought this resolution forward. I believe he is very sincere in what he is proposing. I believe it is not being done for publicity, but that the hon. member is sincere in his intentions with respect to the proposal before us.
I am deeply interested in this question, because I believe that all Canadians in this day and age should be interested in education. The education of our young men and women

today presents a special problem. I am interested because I am a member of the teaching profession-I have been all my life-and because I have seen a great deal of some of the things the hon. member is advocating.
Third, I am interested because in the constituency which I represent is one of Canada's finest universities-a university which is rapidly expanding. I should like to speak briefly about the growth of our university. I can remember 25 years ago attending school at Fredericton at a time when the University of New Brunswick had only 400 students or less. Today that university is filled beyond capacity with over 1,800. That is a situation which exists in practically every school and university across this country.
Even so there are many hundreds and perhaps many thousands of young people who cannot get a university education such as they and this country so vitally need, because of financial circumstances. Every one of us could give from personal experience examples of students who were able to obtain an education because they received just that little bit of extra help. I can well remember a young lad who was in my class at school, a boy who was orphaned at 12. His father was killed in a tragic accident. He was the only boy in the family and when he graduated from high school, having matriculated with high marks, he was able to obtain a Beaverbrook scholarship. At that time the sum of money which this scholarship represented was not very great, but the boy was nevertheless able to go to university and get a degree in electrical engineering. Today he is one of eastern Canada's ablest engineers. It would have been impossible for this boy to have gone on to a university if he had not received this little bit of extra help.
At the present time there is a most important committee sitting in the other place, and the activities of this committee are perhaps the most important of those going on in this parliament at the present time. I refer to the committee on manpower and employment. A short time ago a report was made before that committee by Dr. James, discussing the question of education today. He pointed out plainly that the great bulk of those people who have an employment problem today are those who have received little or no education. The figures put forward are probably accurate,-Dr. James said about 2 per cent of those seeking employment had received university educations. I think perhaps that figure of 2 per cent is a bit high.

As I listened to the introductory remarks of the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) I could not help but feel that the legislation already in existence meets the objectives he advances in this resolution. As the hon. member read letters and telegrams, most of which I believe were dated back in 1954, it occurred to me that the hon. gentleman should have taken them to the then minister of finance of the Liberal government and read them to him. If that course was followed then the hon. member's representations must have fallen on deaf ears because very little was done by the former administration in this field compared with the record of this Conservative government since it came into power in 1957.
To appreciate the record of achievement of the present government one has only to briefly review some of the measures it has introduced. The hon, member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) made mention of the increase in per capita grants for universities from $1 to $1.50. Another significant step taken by the present government is represented by the recent legislation providing for grants to universities for the construction of student residences. The government has now come along with legislation to exempt

Private Bills
tuition fees for income tax purposes. One also recalls the grants that have been given by this government in the training and vocational field. One also thinks of the assistance that has been given for the provision of vocational training for the unemployed in conjunction with the provinces. In the light of this brief review I am very happy to be a member of a government that has seen fit to make such significant contributions to the furtherance of education.
I am pleased to speak in support of the legislation already passed in this field. In my riding we have two important colleges, the only two of their kind in the British commonwealth and second to none in the world, the Ontario agricultural college and the Ontario veterinary college. In my riding we also have MacDonald institute where we train some of the finest wives to be found any place in Canada. The exemption from income tax of tuition fees will be of great assistance to students attending these universities. In brief, I think the aims of the hon. member's resolution have already been met by legislation introduced by this government.
The hon. member's resolution also calls for the exemption from income tax of the cost of textbooks and scientific equipment. I should be happy to see these items included as I am sure the students would who are attending the colleges I have mentioned, but I am afraid a great administrative problem would arise from the implementation of such a provision. The following questions immediately come to my mind. How would you arrive at a means of establishing the deductions? Many textbooks are used over and over again and students often purchase secondhand books. How would you designate what was necessary equipment and what was unnecessary? The equipment used by a student engineer is very different from that used by a medical student. The implementation of such a provision would mean that the department would be confronted with a complex administrative problem.
In conclusion let me say that I am proud of the legislation in this field introduced by this government and I am happy to take this opportunity of congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on doing what has been done thus far.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the resolution supported by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl). I believe that all people in this country today recognize not only the advantage to the individual of higher education but also this country's great need for it.
Not long ago in reading a report from the Canadian medical association I noticed that there was a great need for doctors all across this country. For the last four or five years we have heard much about the great need for engineers. Some of the reports we have read have imbued us with the fear that other countries are exceeding us in the training of technical and professional men.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat praised the work done by his government in increasing university grants. I agree with him in part but in doing so I must also remind the hon. gentleman that it was in 1955 under the former administration that these grants to universities were initiated, then at the rate of 50 cents per capita. A year or two later they were increased to $1 per capita. While the present administration has done a good deal for higher education I think hon. members opposite must not lay claim to the credit for all the interest that has been shown in higher education in Canada over the last few years.
I am interested in the number of times the hon. member for Cartier has placed this resolution on the order paper and in the number of times he has mentioned this subject in the house. Last year in the budget debate he made reference to his contention that there should be some income tax deduction for the expenses of a higher education. After concluding a speech similar to the one the hon. member made today, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), as reported at page 5169 of Hansard of June 20, 1960, said:
As to the matter raised by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl), may I say that this matter was discussed fully last year. He is aware of the additional burden we are carrying in the federal treasury now by reason of our increase from $1 to $1.50 in the per capita federal grants to the universities; that is per capita of population in each province. These are substantial additions that we have undertaken. I think there is little to be gained now in reviewing this question again. It could have been raised in the budget discussion but I do not believe it was raised there. It was discussed fully a year ago and I think the situation has not changed since that time.
That was only approximately a year ago. We now have amendments to the Income Tax Act which I am sure every hon. member will welcome and recognize as desirable.
I do not wish to labour the point but there is one thought I should like to leave with hon. members. I have had some experience in the field of education. It has always been and still is my opinion that in any country that pays attention to its educational system there will always be sufficient care given to the average student.
There are two types of students for whom special care should be undertaken. First, there are those who have the ability to attend

university, and then there are those who have ability far below the average. With respect to those who have ability far below the average the state might just as well train them to do some job because it is going to have to look after them anyway, whether they are children or adults. With respect to those who are above the average in ability, the state should look after them, particularly a democracy which needs that type of leadership in the different professions that these young men are able to fill.
Let us suppose, for example, that a father sends his son to university. Unless he is a very wealthy man he will have to make some sacrifice in order to do that. When the young lad is through university and he goes out to take up a job in whatever field of training he happens to choose he may be a source of great pride to his father, he may be a source of great pride to his own home town; he may have equipped himself to make a good living, but there is one fact that remains. The people who get the greatest advantage out of the training that that young man has acquired is the state itself. If the state is going to get the advantage of that young man's training, then it should be responsible for paying a part of the cost. Whether the method suggested by the hon. member for Cartier is the best method for assisting university students is another matter. It is certainly one way. I myself have some leaning toward a student loan plan, and I believe that a student loan plan would be welcomed in this country provided, of course, that there were no strings attached and those who are actually in need of loans to get themselves through university are able to get them.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, I do recognize the worth of the resolution which we now have before us. I support the hon. member for Cartier in his bringing it forth and I commend him for being so persistent in his idea of trying to provide help for university students in this country.
