ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give early consideration to the advisability of the appointment of a board of engineers for the purpose of studying and reporting upon the linking of the St. Lawrence seaway (river) with the port of New York via the Richelieu river, lake Champlain and the Hudson river.
(Text):
He said: Mr. Speaker, the resolution that is now before the house is not a new one. It has been on the order paper now for three sessions and it has been in the minds of many Canadians as well as many people of the United States for a considerably longer period. However, I am happy to be able to move this resolution this evening in order, not only to be able to describe more fully than I have been able to do up until now

Richelieu Waterway
the Richelieu-Champlain waterway but also to give the house reasons that I feel make the Champlain waterway economically advantageous to Canada.
The Richelieu-Champlain waterway would provide a practicable water route some 400 miles long from the St. Lawrence river in Quebec up the Richelieu river to the international boundary, then across lake Champlain and down the Hudson river to Albany and New York. Hon. members may be interested to know that the Richelieu river, in spite of the many natural obstacles to be found in it, has served Canadians and Canadian-United States commercial traffic ever since 1609. It was only in 1843 that the locks, situated now at St. Ours and the locks in the Chambly canal, were first built. At that time a six-foot barge canal was built and played an important part in the economic development of that area.
The Chambly canal, which marks the southern end of the Canadian section of the waterway, is 11.8 miles long and it has nine consecutive and very antiquated locks with a controlling length of 118 feet and a controlling depth over the sills of 6.5 feet. No major changes have been made to the canal since it was first built, and I think the canal is understandably outmoded and although completely inadequate for modern transportation it is still being used.
One of the pioneers, whom I should like to mention tonight, is Guy Tombs Limited. They have been using this waterway, in spite of the difficulties, for many years and, in order to use it, have had to build special barges. In 1937 the first step toward construction of a practicable water route from the St. Lawrence to New York was the construction of a lock at St. Ours at the northern end of the waterway. It is some 339 feet long, 45 feet wide, with a depth of 12.5 feet over the sills.
At the same time a dam across the Richelieu river at Fryers island was built in order to control the flow of the river and to maintain the level of the waterway in lake Champlain. This dam has not been utilized because the project did not go ahead, but it is a necessary step that has already been taken in order to achieve a practicable water route through the Richelieu river. Except for the dredging of the Richelieu river from six feet to 12 feet which was done in 1946 from Sorel to St. Ours, no major changes were made in the Canadian section of the waterway.
The United States section of this route starts, of course, at the international boundary and goes through lake Champlain to Whitehall, a distance of 112 miles with a controlling depth of 12 feet. From Whitehall to Troy, a

distance of some 63 miles, the depth is 12 feet and from Troy to Albany, a distance of 8.5 miles, the depth is 13-J feet. From Albany to New York, a distance of 143.5 miles, it has a depth of 27 feet. Over the years prior to 1937 a considerable amount of interest had been shown in the Richelieu-Champlain waterway. In 1936 the government of Canada and the government of the United States concurred in referring the project to the international joint commission for study. The commission made its report in 1938, and I should like to place on Hansard the recommendations of the international joint commission, found in the report of that commission on the Champlain waterway, page 17. The recommendations are, and I quote:
-the commission recommends that the present report be considered an interim report, and that it be authorized to retain jurisdiction over the matter until the St. Lawrence waterway has become an accomplished tact and the commission has had an opportunity of studying the effect of its operation upon the proposed Champlain waterway.
There are, of course, two points that must be noted in this recommendation. First of all, it is an interim report of the international joint commission, and not a final report.
Second, the commission recommend that it be authorized to retain jurisdiction over the matter until the St. Lawrence seaway had been completed. Hon. members will agree that in 1938 the St. Lawrence seaway was far from being an accomplished fact. The economic picture of the area involved in the project was very far from being what it is today. For the past 25 years, in spite of the difficulties caused by nine antiquated locks, a canal with a controlling depth of only six feet in the Canadian section and the necessity of specially built barges, an average of 50,000 tons of freight per year has been carried over this route. Over half of that tonnage was newsprint going to New York. The total Richelieu river tonnage including bulk shipments to points in the Richelieu valley delivered by local barges has been as high as 135,000 tons under conditions which can only be described as terrible.
There is no limit to the southbound Quebec newsprint tonnage available. Competent engineers and economists have estimated that there would be 10 to 20 times the present through tonnage to New York if the waterway were enlarged and modernized to permit the passage of modern and practicable canallers. Moreover, with improved transportation facilities, a very considerable amount of ore from the lower St. Lawrence in Quebec and in Labrador would also move along the Richelieu-Champlain waterway to its destination in the United States.
The undertaking and the eventual completion of the St. Lawrence seaway accompanied

by a rapid industrial development on the south shore of the St. Lawrence between Montreal and Sorel accentuated the economic potential of the Richelieu project. It is because of the economic potential and the necessity for Canada to maintain an ever-expanding economy that Canadians, whether as individuals or whether organized in groups such as municipalities, chambers of commerce, boards of trade in Canada or the New York-Vermont interstate commission, have taken an extremely active part in preparing and sending to the government well documented briefs on the economic justifiability of the Richelieu-Champlain waterway. These briefs were the result of studies made first of all of the interim report of the international joint commission of 1937 and subsequent studies made by engineers and economists both in this country and in the United States.
Organizations such as those I mentioned a moment ago have spent considerable time and money from their own resources in a most commendable effort to obtain the economic and technical information necessary with regard to the Canadian as well as the United States section of this waterway. Many of the international meetings were held both in Canada and in the United States on an unofficial but extremely useful basis so as to coordinate the studies of both countries toward this project which can only be realized on an international basis. All of the studies that have been made pointed distinctly and emphatically, if not to an immediate start on the project for which there is as yet no definite plans at least to the advisability of both Canada and the United States undertaking a joint study of the project on a governmental level as they did in 1937 through the international joint commission.
In April of 1957, the United States congress voted an amount of money to begin a study of the project and Canada was invited to take part in that joint study. As a result of a motion I had placed on the order paper, I asked the government to table all the correspondence exchanged between the federal government and the authorities of the state of New York and Washington concerning the Richelieu river waterway which would link the St. Lawrence with the Hudson river. As a result, I was handed sessional paper No. 250, dated Tuesday, April 26, 1960, and I should like to place this on Hansard. On April 30, 1957, the United States embassy in Ottawa sent a letter to the Department of External Affairs which reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Cleveland:
Reference is made to the Department of External Affairs' note No. X-215 of August 15, 1952 and the embassy's note No. 297 of June 3, 1952, concerning the Richelieu river-lake Champlain waterway.
Richelieu Waterway
It will be recalled that in this exchange of notes the Canadian government was asked whether it would join the United States in a request to the international joint commission to re-study this subject with a view to determining the possibilities of deepening the waterway to accommodate 12-foot navigation. In its response, the Department of External Affairs took note of a comment made in a January 4, 1938 report of the international joint commission to the effect that a recommendation concerning the development of the proposed waterway could only be determined after the St. Lawrence waterway had been constructed and put into operation. The Department of External Affairs' note concluded that it would not be appropriate to refer this matter to the international joint commission for further study.
In this connection, the attention of the United States government has recently been invited to resolutions adopted by the general assembly of Vermont and by the city council of Burlington expressing the view that, as a result of the progress that has been made in the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway, it is desirable to have both the United States and Canadian governments ask the international joint commission to renew its investigation and study of the construction of the Richelieu river-lake Champlain waterway.
While the United States government does not wish at this time to propose to the Canadian government that it join with the United States in a renewed reference to the international joint commission, the United States would appreciate ascertaining whether or not the Canadian government's views on this question have changed in any respect since they were last made known in the Department of External Affairs' note No. X-215 of August 15, 1952.
Sincerely yours,
Milton C. Rewinkel, Counselor of Embassy.
There was no answer to this letter that was tabled but on October 30, 1958 the governor of New York namely Averill Harriman sent a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) which reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
The congress of the United States has allocated $15,000 to the United States army corps of engineers for the current fiscal year to begin a study of a possible Richelieu-Champlain waterway. As you know, the 1937 study of the international joint commission determined that such a waterway was engineeringly feasible. The questions of depth (12'-14'-27') and economic benefits now need re-examination.
Because of the recent economic changes in Canada, it is my feeling that a similar study should be made on the Canadian side. If your engineers could initiate a similar undertaking, the two studies could be consolidated into a single substantial report which would certainly point the way for an inland waterway of great economic benefit to both the Dominion of Canada and the state of New York.
Sincerely,
Averill Harriman.
To this letter the Canadian government replied on November 13, 1958, as follows:
My dear Governor:
In the absence of the Prime Minister, I wish to thank you cordially for your letter of October 30, in which you inform the Prime Minister of the action which the U.S. congress has taken

Richelieu Waterway
recently in allocating monies to the U.S. army corps of engineers for the current fiscal year to begin a study of a possible Richelieu-Champlain waterway. May I say that this matter has already been informally drawn to the attention of our department by the department of state.
Yours sincerely,
N. A. Robertson.
On December 22, 1958 the foreign service of the United States sent a letter to the Department of External Affairs of Canada. It is addressed to Mr. Cleveland and it reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Cleveland:
The department of state has requested the embassy to ascertain the present views of the Canadian government concerning possible joint studies of the Richelieu canal-lake Champlain waterway.
In this connection it may be of interest to Canadian authorities that under section 112 of the United States public law 85-500, the secretary of the army was authorized and directed to study a "water route from Albany, New York, into lake Champlain, New York and Vermont, including the advisability of modifying existing federal and state improvements, with due consideration of ultimate connection with the Saint Lawrence River in Canada". The chief of the United States army corps of engineers has initiated the activities in the United States necessary for submission of a report to congress as directed. Consideration of an ultimate connection with the St. Lawrence river would require, of course, the co-operation of appropriate agencies of the Canadian government.
If the Canadian government should find it agreeable to engage in a co-operative or joint study, an established procedure for arrangements, as you know, is available under article IX of the boundary waters treaty of 1909. In such an event the international joint commission could be requested to resume consideration of the reference of January 2, 1936, in which the two governments asked the commission to investigate the advisability of the improvement of a waterway from Montreal through lake Champlain to connect with the Hudson river. Under the reference the commission submitted an interim report to the two governments in 1937. As you will recall, that report recommended, in effect, that no further consideration be given to development of such a waterway until the possibilities could be analysed in relation to an improved channel in the St. Lawrence river.
Alternately, of course, a new reference to the international joint commission could be formulated defining the nature and scope of any study desired at this time. The department of state understands that the department of the army is prepared to move forward with studies of the Champlain waterway in the United States, as well as with joint studies of a possible connection with the St. Lawrence if the Canadian government should deem joint studies desirable. The department of state further understands that the department of the army can adjust within reasonable limits the time and rate of studies in the United States to conform with reviews of the Canadian government regarding any joint studies. It is for this reason, as well as the other considerations cited above, that the embassy would be most appreciative of the general views of the Canadian government.
Sincerely, yours,
Milton C. Rewinkel, Counselor of Embassy.
Almost one year later the Department of External Affairs answered the letter on November 17, 1959:
Dear Mr. Smith:
Since receipt of Mr. Rewinkel's letter of December 22, 1958, concerning studies of the Champlain-Richelieu waterway, this matter has been under further examination.
As you will recall, the Minister of Transport on June 11, 1959, read in the House of Commons an extract from an interim report which had been made to him on this subject. This extract read as follows:
"The previous cost estimates are now being revised in the light of recent alternative plans and present day costs by the Department of Public Works, and when these are completed, some estimate can be made of the volume of traffic required to justify improvements to the present canals and studies will be made to determine probable traffic available".
The cost revisions are proceeding but it is not possible to say, at this moment, when the results will be ready.
Yours sincerely,
J. H. Cleveland,
American Division.
Several things become clear as a result of the correspondence I have just read. First of all, that very little interest has been shown by the government in the project. Second, the government had no intention of undertaking a joint study with the United States of the project which could have meant a possible government expenditure for Canada of some $15,000. I strongly suspect that the private organizations in Canada to which I referred a while ago have spent two or three times that amount in the preparation of the economic and engineering studies that they had made at their own expense.
But the government did not even include one cent in the estimates for the study of the project over the past three years, as is evidenced by the remarks by the then minister of transport which are to be found in Hansard of June 11, 1959, on page 4565. In speaking to the hon. member for Laurier the then minister of transport had this to say:
The hon. member spoke about the Richelieu canal, and I should like to read him a short report made to me by the members of our economics division and the public works engineers who are working on this project at the present time. It reads as follows:
From there it goes on to the part that was included in the correspondence I have just read. Then the hon. member for Laurier said:
May I ask who are the members of the committee dealing with this matter?

These are the terms of reference under which they are working. First of all, we are trying to find out what the economic justification might be for proceeding with work of this kind, and the probable engineering costs.
From all appearances the government has chosen to utilize the engineers and the economists that are already in the departments, without having a special study made of this project. I have certainly the greatest respect for the engineers and economists in the departments, but I respectfully submit that with the amount of work that they have in the Department of Transport and in the Department of Public Works it would be almost impossible for them to make the thorough study that such a huge project would require.
All through the discussion of the Champlain waterway in the reports and studies a most confusing and exasperating veil of secrecy was drawn over the whole subject and it became absolutely impossible for members of the opposition to obtain any information as to what type of study was being carried out and who had the responsibility of carrying out these particular studies.
If you refer to Hansard of February 4, 1960, you will have an idea of what I mean when I say it was impossible to obtain any information as to the work or study that was being carried out. At page 717 of Hansard I am reported as having asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) this question:
Now that the Prime Minister has had an opportunity of travelling along, if not on, the Richelieu river from Sorel to the United States border, can he say whether a study of the economic and technical feasibility of the Richelieu waterway is under way or is being contemplated by the government?

Then at page 866 of Hansard for February 9, 1960 I am reported as having asked this question:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. On Thursday last I asked him whether the government was making a study of the economic and technical feasibility of the Richelieu waterway, and the Prime Minister answered that when the last government was in
Richelieu Waterway
power there was an investigation which was still under way. Did the Prime Minister mean that the government has asked the international joint commission to resume the investigation the commission was carrying out and which was interrupted until the St. Lawrence seaway had been completely finished?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as in the past, several departments are engaged in this work.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext: May I direct another question to the Prime Minister. I did not get the chance to put this as a supplementary to the questions asked a while ago. Would the Prime Minister inform the house to what department questions on the Richelieu waterway could be addressed, and which department has responsibility for the study mentioned in the Prime Minister's statement?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if questions are directed to me I will see that they are redirected to the proper department.
In the light of this exchange I think the Prime Minister will forgive me if I entertain certain suspicions that no serious consideration has been given to the project of the Richelieu waterway.
Yet on December 7 the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) announced the results of the studies the government claims had been continuing in several departments. The minister did not of course make the announcement in the House of Commons, where the subject had been brought up on innumerable occasions. The minister chose to make the announcement at a banquet given by the Montreal board of trade and la cham-bre de commerce at the close of a day's conference on the Richelieu-Champlain waterway. By an extraordinary coincidence the study of the project, which according to the Prime Minister had been going on for some years, just happened to finish in time for the banquet, because otherwise the Prime Minister would surely have seen to it that the rights and prerogative of parliament were preserved and the decision made known to the House of Commons first.
During the whole day of the conference on December 7 the members of the conference-and that included members of the United States congress-had listened to well prepared and well documented briefs read by competent people who had been interested in the project for several years. There had been a great deal of enthusiasm, hope and interest shown, and it was unanimously agreed that the very least that could be done would be for the Canadian government and the United States government to engage in a joint study on a program.
One of the speakers at the conference was Mr. Holubowicz from the port of New York authority. His statement can in no way be

Richelieu Waterway
considered as an exaggerated, or ill-thought out one. I think it is a very moderate and useful statement and 1 should like to put it on record in Hansard at this time. It is taken from a copy of a speech he made on December 7 at a meeting in Montreal of the Quebec chamber of commerce and it reads as follows:
At this point, perhaps it will be helpful for me to recapitulate for you the attitude of the principal United States proponents of the Champlain waterway study.
It should be understood clearly that the efforts being carried out in the United States are limited for the present to the carrying out of a comprehensive study of the project, and not at obtaining authorization on or funds for any actual improvement as yet. At present, no one has sufficient information or technical data on which to base a judgment as to the economic feasibility or justification of any improvement. There has been talk of a 12 ft., 14 ft., 16 ft., 27 ft., and even a 35 ft. waterway. Obviously, no judgment can be made as to which of these depths should be provided, or for that matter whether any improvement at all can be justified, until a full study is completed, which will, among other things, relate economic benefit to the cost of construction.
Therefore, our point of view is that a comprehensive study is needed, similar in scope to the study conducted by the international joint commission in 1937. In our opinion, this is a rational and sound approach to the problem of development.
He concludes by saying:
Many interests in the United States are hopeful that the Canadian government will decide to join in studying this project which holds out such a great promise for the economic future of both our countries. We earnestly believe that if competent studies indicate the need for improvement of this transportation artery it would form yet another link between our two countries and do much to enhance the friendship and spirit of cooperation that now exists between us.
That was one of the points of view put forward at the conference. There was, also, another viewpoint which was put forward by Lieutenant Colonel Dansereau, a member of the international joint commission. He had this to say as reported in La Presse of December 7, 1960.
(Translation):
It is certainly possible to come to an agreement with the United States in the near future concerning 12 feet navigation on the Richelieu river.
(Text):
I have every reason to believe Lieutenant Colonel Dansereau because last summer I attended a meeting of the New York interstate commission which was discussing the project, and at a dinner which was given the governor of Vermont, Governor Stafford, stated toward the end of his speech that Vermont was ready to go ahead with the project but was waiting to see what steps the Canadian government proposed to take. On December 7, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) answered the governor of Vermont in no uncertain terms. The hon. gentleman answered the interstate commission, the

board of trade and all those who were interested when he said at that banquet, and I quote from page 3 of:
(Translation):
Excerpts from a speech delivered by the Hon. Leon Balcer, Minister of Transport, before the chamber of commerce of the province of Quebec, in Montreal, on December 7, 1960.
I quote from page 3:
In my capacity as Minister of Transport, I should have liked to be able to inform you tonight that the federal government is willing to carry out such a project without delay, or still that we have decided to have the matter carefully looked into by the boundary waters commission. Unfortunately, I am not in a position to make such a statement, but this does not mean however that the government and my department in particular are not following with great interest the work accomplished by you people and that they are not impressed by the enthusiasm and interest shown in this project by such responsible people as you.
(Text):
The kindest thing I can say about the minister's statement that night is that it is the bluntest brush-off I have ever heard a minister of the crown address to any group. On page 7 of that same extract, the Minister of Transport had this to say, and I quote: (Translation):
The problem that the government, and more particularly the Department of Transport, have to face is to make the most of the taxpayers' money, with only one purpose in mind, to give public interest precedence over all other interests. (Text):
That is a very profound and acceptable statement, but it is extremely difficult to see the application of that principle by a government which is willing to spend, for instance, $5,500,000 on military bands in this country but which refuses to pay some $15,000 for a joint study of the economic advantages to be derived from one of the country's economic assets at a time when our standard of living and prosperity depends so essentially upon our capacity for keeping our economy continually expanding. The government's attitude reminds me of a modern version of fiddling while Rome burns.
After the announcement in Montreal by the Minister of Transport of the government's policy with regard to Richelieu-Champlain waterway it was only natural that members of the opposition should try to obtain some pertinent information with respect to the study which was supposed to have been made by the government. Together with the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) and others, I wanted to know, for instance, who had made the reports; what alternative routes had been studied; at what different depths had the project been considered; what consultations had taken place with the United States in connection

with a project which is international in scope; on what basis was the potential volume of traffic on the waterway estimated; and, lastly, what was the estimated cost of the alternative routes and the depths of those waterways.
In order to get some information which I felt was of public interest a motion was made for the tabling of the report, but here again a cloak of secrecy fell once more over the report, this time not by means of doubletalk but in the form of a procedural technicality-it was argued that interdepartmental reports are considered confidential and cannot be tabled. The result was that the house was given no information whatever on the type of study which had been made and was asked to accept that the project is not economically feasible in spite of several available reports to the contrary.

It seems to me our present and future economic difficulties and our unemployment problem will not be solved by one over-all solution. It will be necessary to study general economic and unemployment problems in terms of specific solutions for specific problems in specific areas. Although it is certainly commendable it is not sufficient to determine and to define distressed areas in our economy which must be given special help. This, of course, is good and needed but can only be considered an emergency measure to prevent the possible economic collapse of these areas. If we are to really ensure continued over-all prosperity by means of a continuing expanding economy we must pinpoint and utilize to the fullest possible extent all the natural assets with which our country has been so readily endowed.
I submit that the Richelieu river being connected with lake Champlain and the Hudson river is one of Canada's natural assets which could definitely bolster our economy and help to keep our economy growing. Although the government may be reluctant to give the basis on which it claims the Richelieu-Champlain waterway is not economically feasible, I have no hesitation in putting forth the arguments which I feel make the waterway not only feasible but a necessity if we are to exploit our natural assets intelligently and strengthen our overall economy.
I mentioned earlier the rapid industrial expansion that is taking place between Montreal and Sorel. speechtext:
I thank hon. members for giving me extra time. I will try to conclude as quickly as I can.
As I was saying, in the past 10 years on the south shore between Montreal and Sorel a considerable number of heavy industries have flourished. There is, for instance, Quebec Iron and Titanium which started to roll in 1950. The Steel Company of Canada is now established there. Others include Quebec Titanium Pigment, St. Maurice Chemicals, the ore reduction plant at Contrecoeur and Crucible Steel of Canada. British Titanium Pigments are now constructing a huge plant and plans for a rolling mill are being prepared. The result of all this is that the mouth of the Richelieu river falls within a highly industrialized area. Furthermore, there is east of Montreal and Sorel the paper mills and the ore mines on the north shore of Quebec and Labrador.
The present water transportation systems between this highly industrialized section of western Quebec and the industrialized section of the United States immediately to the south are (a) a very long, circuitous water route by the gulf of St. Lawrence and the Atlantic ocean, some 1,800 miles in length, or (b) the present six-foot waterway by way of the Richelieu river, a distance of some 650 miles.
A practicable waterway on the Richelieu would reduce the distance between the industrialized sections of Quebec and the United States by well over 1,000 miles. Adequate and modern canals and lakes on the Richelieu would mean a substantial reduction in transportation cost and would greatly increase the quantity and variety of the tonnage now moving on the Richelieu.

If the Richelieu were properly canalized it may be expected that there would be a large tonnage of concentrates to New Jersey, a greatly increased tonnage of newsprint, a substantial quantity of pig iron from the ore reduction plants and quantities of lumber, and wood pulp. There would also be quantities of semi-finished steels moving on the Richelieu. It may be expected that the northbound traffic would comprise raw cotton, clay products, raw sugar, molding sand, phosphate rock and structural steel.
It was estimated in 1949 that with a 12-foot waterway the total tonnage on the Richelieu waterway would aggregate two million tons. With the unexpected industrial development of the past 10 years in that area I am convinced that the aggregate tonnage would be far greater than that. I cannot help but think that the government judged the project as economically unfeasible on the basis of the present tonnage moving on the six-foot waterway and on the basis of the incalculable obstacles to transportation. Surely the government could not have taken into account the industrial expansion that has taken place in the area since the international joint commission made its report in 1937. I submit that the whole south shore from Montreal to Sorel within 10 to 15 years will become the Pittsburgh of Canada in the heavy iron and steel industries.
I hope the government does not believe that additional tonnage on the waterway can be achieved under the present impossible conditions that obtain there. Even the government, I think, must agree that increased traffic on the waterway and industrial expansion will follow the development of the waterway but cannot and will not precede it. I feel that an appropriate and adequate waterway would not only increase the tonnage of traffic on the Richelieu but would encourage the building of secondary industries along the seaway and give rise to a great increase in the number of tourists by yachts. This in itself is also becoming an important industry. In turn this would promote innumerable service trades on the shores of the Richelieu. Canada cannot and should not ignore any of these potential developments at this time.
Having stated some of the reasons why I feel that the Richelieu waterway is not only economically justifiable but even advisable at this time-an opinion which is shared by economists and engineers both in Canada and the United States-I should like to say a few words concerning the possible routes of the waterway.
To my mind, of all the routes that have been considered over the years and recently, the natural route, that of following the Richelieu river to meet the St. Lawrence

river at Sorel offers the greatest advantage both from an economic and an engineering point of view. I believe that the work that was started in 1937 to build a 12-foot waterway to Sorel should be completed as a first step. Then, if outbound and inbound traffic directed to Montreal from the United States would not foul up shipping on the St. Lawrence river, a cut-off from St. Jean to Laprairie might be constructed as a second step. The reasons I have to support my suggestions are to be found in the international joint commission interim report on the Champlain waterway at page 15, where the commission's conclusions are set out, as follows:
That there are five possible routes for a waterway from Montreal to the Hudson river by way of lake Champlain, the last mentioned being an all-water route and the remainder overland routes, as follows:
(a)	From lake St. Francis on the St. Lawrence river to lake Champlain via the Chazy river.
(b)	From lake St. Francis to the Richelieu river three miles south of the city of St. Johns.
(c)	From Caughnawaga, on the St. Lawrence river, to Fryer's island on the Richelieu river.
(d)	From the St. Lawrence at Longueuil to Fryer's island on the Richelieu river.
(e)	From the St. Lawrence river at Sorel up the Richelieu river to lake Champlain.
In the case of all five routes the existing waterway would be followed through lake Champlain and by way of the Champlain canal to the Hudson river at Albany.
That of these five routes, the last mentioned (e) is the most practicable from an engineering standpoint and the least impracticable from an economic point of view.
As a second reason for supporting my suggestion I would say that this particular route is the only all water route of all those that I have mentioned. Recently there has also been talk of a canal between St. Jean and Laprairie, but that also would be an overland route and I shall have something more to say about that particular suggestion in a minute.
One of the strongest reasons for the suggestion I have made is that the greatest volume of traffic now contemplated would come from points below Montreal and the access to the Richelieu river at Sorel is not only unencumbered, but it also offers the shortest route to in-shipping coming from points east of Montreal and destined for New York.
The fourth reason is that when the St. Lawrence seaway was first planned the canal was to pass on the Montreal side of the St. Lawrence. However, subsequently the plans were changed and the canal now passes on the south shore. A canal from St. Jean to Laprairie would necessarily fall in the St. Lawrence seaway traffic and as there are enough tie-ups in the St. Lawrence seaway, any cross traffic on the seaway should be considered very seriously.
Richelieu Waterway
My fifth reason is, as I said earlier, that Lieutenant Colonel Dansereau, who is a member of the international joint commission, stated that the United States was ready to go ahead with a 12-foot waterway and, from what I have heard on the subject from United States spokesmen I have every reason to believe that the United States would be ready to proceed with a 12-foot canal, but they do not at this time consider a 27-foot waterway.
If a canal is to be dug from St. Jean to Laprairie to my mind, it should be a 27-foot canal if it is going to have any economic value at all. However, a 12-foot waterway with adequate locking facilities could and would at this time immeasurably increase tonnage of traffic on the Richelieu and help the industrial expansion in the Richelieu valley, which in turn would contribute to Canada's over-all economic expansion until a 27-foot waterway is considered by both the United States and Canada and a 27-foot canal can be dug from St. Jean to Lapraire.
The Richelieu waterway is not the only national asset Canada possesses, and since we have to find a way to further expand our economy, then the Richelieu seaway and other such projects should be proceeded with without delay.
In solving the unemployment problem, short term measures must necessarily have to be taken into account, but the real solution of the unemployment problem is to plan for and create an atmosphere and conditions which will facilitate our industrial expansion, create more jobs and expand our economy.
Up until the announcement was made by the Minister of Transport on December 7, I, and many Canadians, had entertained very high hopes that the Richelieu-Champlain waterway would start almost immediately. I recall the summer of 1959, I think it was, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) was making his political tour of the province of Quebec. He stopped off at Sorel for the purpose of examining the waterway and from all appearances he seemed to be very much impressed by it. In the report that appeared in the Canadian Shipping and Marine Engineering News of January, 1960. Mr. Plummer had this to say, and I quote:
At the conclusion of his inspection trip, the Prime Minister confided to the federated chamber of commerce heads and delegates accompanying him and to Dr. L. G. Tombs (vice president of Guy Tombs Limited, Montreal), chairman of the navigable waterways committee of la chambre de commerce de la province de Quebec:
"You may rest assured that if this project is capable of realizing a spur to the prosperity of the nation, it shall be studied with all the attention it merits."
In the light of what the Minister of Transport said on December 7 we are faced once

Richelieu Waterway
again with the difference that exists between the Prime Minister's words and the government's action. It was very disappointing to those who were at the conference to hear that the government not only did not intend to start work on the project but was not even willing to go ahead with a joint study of the project through the international joint commission.
In this resolution, Mr. Speaker, I am asking not for a start immediately on construction of the seaway but for a serious study to be made by appointing a board of engineers to study, in connection with a United States board of engineers, the project so as to determine whether it is economically feasible. I am convinced that any study of that kind would show that the Richelieu waterway would be economically advantageous to Canada. If the government does not reconsider its decision of not having a full scale study made of the project, not only will it be brushing off countless citizens who have been interested in this project for many years but it will also be brushing off an opportunity to facilitate our industrial expansion, create employment and contribute to Canada's economic growth.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when reference is made to the Richelieu seaway, one should at least take time to study the matter and learn what it is all about, because according to what the previous speaker said, it is obvious that he did not know what he was talking about.
(Text):
I should now like to come back to the subject under consideration by the house, if I may be allowed to do so. The first thing I should like to do is to congratulate the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) who made an excellent presentation of this resolution this evening. During the course of at least 60 minutes he indicated to the house not only that he understood the purport of the resolution but also that he knew whereof he spoke.
It seems to me that this is a simple resolution. All it does is to ask the government to set up a board of engineers to consider the feasibility of the route from the St. Lawrence to New York via the Richelieu river and lake

Champlain. That is not asking such a terrible thing. The government from time to time, sets up commissions of this kind.
The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres during the course of his remarks has indicated that this is a matter which would cost perhaps something in the neighbourhood of $15,-
000.	When one realizes that not only the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) but the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) and the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Com-tois) went down to the area and when they were there certainly led the people to believe that something would be done about this waterway. A year or two or more has gone by, and absolutely nothing is being done about the matter.
What is the position? Why should this resolution not be agreed to? Why should not the government give immediate consideration to this resolution and implement it? The international joint commission in a report referred to by the hon. member for Richelieu-Ver-cheres which was brought down in 1937 made it quite clear, and that is an answer to the question put by the hon. member for Carle-ton (Mr. Bell), that until the St. Lawrence seaway had been completed the commission asked for permission to suspend the whole matter and when the St. Lawrence seaway was completed then consideration should be given to the project. That is all that is being asked by those of us who sit on this side of the house. There is nothing contradictory in what the hon. member has said to what was done by those who were in office prior to the present administration.
The St. Lawrence seaway has now had two complete years of operation and in my opinion they have been two successful years of operation. Why then has not the time arrived-to use the language of the international joint commission-to give consideration to this matter? It is an international project. It is one which requires the concurrence of both the government of the United States and the government of Canada. It is a matter in which several states south of the border are interested. It is a matter in which, north of the border, the province of Quebec has a particular interest.
As the situation stands now I am informed on good authority-and I believe this to be the case-that a large sum of money has been set aside by the United States government authorizing the United States corps of engineers to make borings and studies of the whole project. In fact the United States corps of engineers since this government has been in office have obtained information in connection with this project in relation to the territory of Canada. If that is the case and if the information which I have is correct, then

there is no reason why those who sit on the other side of the house should not co-operate with the United States corps of engineers in setting up a board which would study the economics of this route.
The government is giving consideration to and is studying the Ottawa river waterway. That is a subject which several of us who sit on this side of the house have approved. We think that a study of the Ottawa river or of the canalization of the Ottawa river is one which should be undertaken and I believe that the government has given consideration to it.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext: It is doing it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext:
If it is doing it in so far as the Ottawa river is concerned, why not do it equally in so far as the Richelieu river is concerned down to the United States boundary? It would cost much less to study the economics of the Richelieu than it would to study those of the other routes, although that consideration should not make any difference. Both of them will be linked to the St. Lawrence in this way: one will be moving its traffic down to the St. Lawrence and the other will derive a great deal of its traffic from the St. Lawrence. If the one is a matter which should be studied by this house, it strikes me that the other is also a matter which should be studied.
Another question which comes to my mind is this. What should the board study? The board should study the various routes. It should study the cost and it should study the economics of this waterway. The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres referred to five routes that were considered by the report of the international joint commission. Because they are now known to the house I shall not go into those routes except to say this. Since the report of 1937 was made the economy of the province of Quebec in that area has changed completely. It has changed in so far as the St. Lawrence seaway is concerned. It has changed in so far as the development of the north shore as well as the south shore of the St. Lawrence is concerned. With the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway and the building of the two turning basins in the Laprairie basin, it is now only a short distance from either of those two turning basins to the city of St. Johns. It may be some nine miles, 10 miles or 11 miles.
The experience we gathered from the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway was that excavation costs in the dry were, of course, much less than dredging costs. That is a reason why this study should be undertaken, namely to ascertain which of these five routes,
Richelieu Waterway
six routes or more is the most economical one having regard to circumstances as we find them today.
Then the potential is entirely different. It is the discovery of iron ore in the mines of Labrador and of northern Quebec that tilted the balance in favour of the St. Lawrence seaway. Since iron ore has been discovered, two railways have been constructed on the north shore, one from Schefferville to Seven Islands and another from Gagnon to Port Cartier. Several developments of not only iron ore but by-products coming from the manufacture of ore have resulted in industry being established in the triangle of Montreal-Sorel-Beauharnois. Because of that the potential of the Richelieu cut-off is far greater in 1961 than it ever was in 1937, when this report was made.
I need not tell this house that water transportation is perhaps the cheapest form of transportation in the world. That was one of the main reasons why the great lakes system was developed, in order to bring the inland carriers down to the ports of Montreal and the St. Lawrence river.
Here we have inland ships carrying large cargoes that used to come down to Port Colborne and Prescott for transshipment who because of the construction of a 27-foot channel through the international section of the St. Lawrence river are able to come right down with their huge cargoes, thereby reducing the cost of transportation tremendously.
Such will be the case also if there is development of the Richelieu-Champlain cut-off. Whether it be 14 feet or whether it be more there can be no doubt that the cost of transportation by water of the iron ore, if such be the case, or the products derived from iron ore, or titanium, or such other industries as have been established at Contrecoeur, Va-rennes and Sorel, from the St. Lawrence either by way of Montreal or Sorel will be much lower than the cost of transporting them by rail or even by sea, since the difference is 1,000 miles greater along the coast of the Atlantic ocean.
Therefore it seems to me that this project is one that should commend itself to the house. It should commend itself to the house for another reason, because I believe that if a board of engineers were to find in favour of the economics of this project they would recommend it on a self-liquidating basis. They would of necessity have to treat it in the same way as the St. Lawrence seaway was treated, namely that the cost of construction, whether it be $50 million or more, should be repaid by the imposition of tolls. It would of course be illogical, in my opinion-and I may

Richelieu Waterway
be mistaken-to have tolls on the St. Lawrence river and not the Richelieu, which because of the amount of the expenditure involved would of course be much less than now obtaining on the St. Lawrence canals.
The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres has indicated the attitude of the government. I hold in my hand a memorandum which was presented to the Prime Minister by a delegation which waited upon him in June of 1958, which sets out the reasons why this project should be completed. I know that this submission was well received at the time. Not only was it well received by the Prime Minister, but it was also well received by those of his ministers who are from the province of Quebec. I am somewhat surprised that the Minister of Transport is not in his seat this evening. I presume he has other business of importance to attend to, otherwise he would be here. But I am glad to see that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys is here, because this is his district and he has already declared himself in the matter.
I hold in my hand a clipping which appeared in La Presse of October 28, 1957, entitled:
(Translation):
The digging of the Richelieu channel to a depth of 12 feet.
(Text):
And, in quotes:
(Translation):
"Absolutely necessary", states the Hon. Paul Comtois.
(Text):
And, a little further down in the report, this is what follows:
(Translation):
The Hon. Paul Comtois, minister of mines in the Diefenbaker government, stated that this "project is absolutely necessary for the economic life of the Richelieu area".
"If I am given the opportunity of contributing to the success of that undertaking", went on the representative of Nicolet-Yamaska in the commons, I shall consider it my duty to associate myself to all those who are promoting it."
And a little later on, in quotation marks, always quoting the minister:
"It is certain that we need that seaway", added Mr. Comtois, who referred to it as a "magnificent project", which is of great interest to us.
(Text):
I congratulate the minister and commend him for the statement which he made. It is an excellent statement and one that I am sure would receive favourable comment from not only his own constituents but all those who reside in the area. However I must tell the minister that he could not have had a great deal of influence with his colleague the Minister of Transport, because the Minister of Transport made it quite clear when he spoke at this banquet in Montreal that no
[Mr. Chevrier.l
action was to be taken by the government. Not only did he say that no action was to be taken by the government, but he found that the study indicated that the economics were against the project. Having said that the least that could be done by the Minister of Transport would be to produce in the House of Commons the study which indicates this so we would know why the government came to that conclusion.
But when the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres moved to have produced the papers there was complete secrecy; the government fell back on the question of interdepartmental papers which are not producible. If that is the case the minister should not be making the statements that he does make. After all, if it is a fact that the economics are against the project let us see what the economics say. Surely the house has a right to know on what basis and on what foundation the minister places himself when he makes statements of that character.
It is quite clear to those of us who sit on this side of the house that the government has no intention of implementing this project either by way of construction or by way of the establishment of a board of engineers. The least that the government could and should do is to set up a board of engineers to study the question so that we would know which of the five routes is feasible, the cost of the route, the savings in transportation costs and whether or not the project is justified economically.
But they will not set up a board. They tell us the economics are against the project, and they will not produce the documents to substantiate this. But they go down to the area and get the people all excited, as they did in the 1957 and 1958 campaign. They went across this country from region to region, from province to province, and indicated to many people in Canada that they were going to carry out a number of great projects. However, when they got into the house many of those projects fell flat, just as this one is now falling flat. I can tell the members of the government that the people who reside in this area are not going to forget all the fuss and thunder made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and those associated with him when they went down to the area and certainly led the public to believe that something was going to be done.
At least, if a board of engineers had been established surely there could have been no criticism in the house; surely there could have been no objection to a measure which would have cost somewhere in the neighbourhood of $15,000. That is why I say the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres was

well advised in moving the resolution which he did, and if the government is ready to vote on this, then let us have the vote because then we shall let parliament decide whether hon. members opposite were justified in acting as they did, and whether the motion of my hon. friend the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres was well founded.
Again I commend him for having given the time and study which he has to this subject, along with the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis). Both these hon. members have spent a great deal of time in studying not only the economics but the historical aspects of this project.

speechtext:
The hon. member who sponsored the resolution, and the former minister of transport are very anxious for a vote on this resolution and I just thought that speaking for our party we would support the resolution, not with any particular enthusiasm for what might come beyond it because we cannot really say, but the resolution does seem to ask for something fairly moderate and within range-it is only a question of a board of engineers.
In so far as the actual project is concerned, it seems to me some part of Canada is always being captivated by some great public works project which is going to make that region bloom like a rose. I know we had a great dream at Port Arthur of what the seaway was going to do for us. I understand there are people around Saint John who have a great dream of what the Chig-necto canal is going to do for them and the K. C. Irving interests. I know that my colleague from Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and his friends have great hopes for Moosonee
Richelieu Waterway
as an industrial port once $50 million or $100 million have been devoted to it. I know the hon. member for Carleton looks forward to the day when he can look out on to the new driveway along the Ottawa river and see heavy tankers and ore barges transporting material here and everywhere. These are all dreams which members of parliament, particularly in their own regions, never go against, but I should just like to suggest we might be realistic enough to allow one grandiose project every five years.
I will give this government credit for initiating a grandiose project in the South Saskatchewan dam. John R. MacNicol, a Toronto man, was a great enthusiast and supporter of this project. He used to come into a library where I worked and look up files and records referring to it. He said: They will not listen in Ottawa but some day they will and we shall have that dam. He said: It will change the whole face of the prairies; it will make Saskatchewan the garden of the west. And on he went.
This is grand stuff, part of the Canadian tradition, but we come down to the fact that so many of these grandiose dreams when they become reality are not quite as fine as we expect. I see the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Campbell) in the house and, of course, the former minister of transport came from Stormont, and we know that Cornwall, the city of Stormont, was affected very much by the St. Lawrence seaway. We know that Cornwall is not as prosperous as it was a few years ago because of the St. Lawrence seaway.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext: No. May I interrupt the hon. member to tell him that if Cornwall is not as prosperous today it is not because of the St. Lawrence seaway but because of other and very different reasons.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext:
My point is that we get these grand dreams. To read Creighton's book "The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence", Montreal has been dreaming of shipping to both the American and the western market ever since the 1780's and 1790's. The whole of the canal building along the St. Lawrence, the Welland canal, the railway to the west, all these things were designed to make Montreal the centrepiece of the Canadian economy and I should like to suggest that while it has made a great contribution, today the shift in transport is towards other means rather than water. I would like to suggest that those people who see canals as being a great solution to any area's economy perhaps are probably 50 or 60 years behind the times. It seems to me we should be looking more to airports and facilities in that line or smoothing out of railway problems, or

Richelieu Waterway
better highways for our trucks because I cannot believe that water shipping and the difference today in the return you get from it is really that vital. I know that if you get grain shipped to the west by water and rail, or by all rail there is very little advantage in it. It has been one of the great complaints of the prairie provinces that despite the fact you have the St. Lawrence seaway and shipping right to the heart of the country you cannot get freight moved from east to west with the savings you might expect.
All I am saying really is that it seems to me we as Canadians have tended to overexaggerate the importance to our economy of these advances in the building of canals and waterways just as we have tended to do the same thing to some extent in the case of railways. I think it is about time we looked more toward highways and airports which seem to me to fit into a more rounded picture of transportation at this time.
But this leads me away from the resolution, and to return to it we would support the resolution although not with any tremendous enthusiasm for the project as it seems to stand here, but in the hope that a good report would indicate to us more solidly the economic and other advantages of the scheme.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intended to make a rather elaborate speech, but I see that time flies and that the people from the west are taking over the Richelieu. I shall therefore be brief.
I would be angry with myself if I went right to the point without referring to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm who for us has become the inevitable member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, the petulant and childish member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. I know he will not ask me to retract my words, because he is not aware of their meaning.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext: You are following in the footsteps of the hon. member for Laurier.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext:
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm made a speech in which he strayed away-I would not say from the track-but from the river.
The hon. member told us how proud he was that his chief, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker), visited the Richelieu river in September 1959, to see what was going on there.
Once again, we realize that the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm should have been better informed before speaking.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext: I was on the spot.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext:
Yes, the hon. member was there and I shall tell him what he saw.
When the Prime Minister left Ottawa he told the newspaper correspondents that he was going to sail down the Richelieu to see the possibilities of digging a channel in that beautiful waterway.
He was due to arrive at Sorel. Everybody was waiting. The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm was waiting too.
At a given time, about 3 p.m., according to a report published in La Presse of September 22, 1959, the crowd massed on the banks saw the ferry arriving. "There he is", the people said. The member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm comes first and shouts: "Hail! Here comes the great man." Well, instead of the Prime Minister there came two big Percherons, again according to the report of La Presse.
Do you know what happened afterwards Mr. Speaker, while the member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm and his friends were waiting for their leader? It happened that the Prime Minister came two hours late. He was them put aboard a small craft which took him on a small 20-minute tour and left him on the other shore. He then got into a blue convertible and was driven to the Quebec region where he made political speeches all the way. He completely forgot the Richelieu river.
That is what happened in September 1959 and I thank the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm for having given me this opportunity to recall such an occasion.
Mr. Speaker, now I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) who made tonight in this House of Commons a truly serious speech including complete statistics and a careful documentation.
The proposed Richelieu waterway is a project worth doing. The hon. member's speech stands out against the remarks made on the other side of the house.
It is in fact a serious matter. Mr. Speaker, the member for Richelieu-Vercheres knows what he is talking about. He lives in a constituency bordering the Richelieu river. He does not live on the shore of the small Assomption river. He knows the Richelieu and, besides, he represents here the constituency so named.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext: That is an insult to the people of the Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm constituency.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext: The fact that you are here.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext: I am not changing ridings, and do not worry, I will not move.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext:
Anyway, if you stay there you will die there.
So, Mr. Speaker, I was saying that the member for Richelieu-Vercheres, who lives m a bordering constituency, takes an interest in the waterway. Tonight, you have heard in this house the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres and the former minister of transport, the member for Laurier, who set forth to the house the serious reasons in support of the waterway.
What did the government members offer us? I say it is an insult to the province of Quebec that from the Conservative side, we hear nothing but a Pigeon.
Some members opposite have responsibilities. While the matter of the deepening of the Richelieu river, which concerns his department, is being discussed, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) is not even in his seat. The member for the neighbouring constituency of Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Johnson) whose riding borders on the Richelieu river, is not even in his seat tonight. The member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Comtois), the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, who makes high-sounding electoral statements throughout the province, suggesting that the Richelieu waterway is an important matter, is in his seat tonight, but he is almost asleep while the matter is being discussed in this house.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext: You are very polite.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext:
And just where is the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny), whose constituency borders on the Richelieu river? He is nowhere to be found, he is elsewhere.
While we, on behalf of our area, call for the deepening of the Richelieu river, something which would attract industries and provide jobs for Canadians in that area, as the member for Richelieu-Vercheres has made abundantly clear earlier, while we argue in this house for this waterway, while we call for action and deeds, we note that the Associate Minister of National Defence who is directly concerned in this waterway, because his constituency is next to the Richelieu river and he is a resident of the province of Quebec, made the following statement as reported in this evening's issue of La Presse:
In my riding, I organize dances, fashion shows, etc.; under the Roman empire, you know how the Caesars ruled over their subjects: "with bread and games". When no bread was available, then games were organized. You know that the federal government is unable to grant all kinds of favours. If there is no bread, then there will be games.
I believe it is time the province of Quebec realized that the ministers in the present gov-
Richelieu Waterway
ernment do not represent the aspirations of our province.
In fact, when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) came to the Queen Elizabeth hotel last December to address the members of the chambers of commerce gathered for a day's study of the deepening of the Richelieu river, he threw cold water on the enthusiasm of those who have worked for years towards the implementation of this great project. The Minister of Transport came before the members of the chambers of commerce saying: "I have an interesting statement to make." Here is the statement: "You may be hoping that the government is going to ask the international joint commission to consider the deepening of the river, but unfortunately, I cannot tell you that it will."
Well, Mr. Speaker, in the Liberal party, and I am happy to recall it tonight to the house, we have members who look after the interests of their area. They look after the interests of their province, while the member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Johnson) never said a word in favour of the waterway. He is not even here tonight, when we are discussing that matter, one which affects each and every elector in Chambly-Rouville.
When the Minister of Transport is absent, when the Associate Minister of National Defence is absent, we, Liberals, rise in this house to say that we have been active.
The member for Richelieu-Vercheres and I went to the United States to attend the interstate conference in the state of New York. In 1959, we went to the interstate conference in Vermont, and to the 1960 conference, again in Vermont-

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext: Neither of you did much.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext:
-where we have met engineers, American experts and the governor of Vermont who told us why they were for the immediate deepening of the Richelieu river and lake Champlain. Not so long ago, we went to a town in our ridings and called a meeting of six members from ridings bordering on the river.
We explained to them the reasons in favour of the Richelieu waterway. We asked the Quebec provincial government that the committee or the Quebec board of economic planning look into the economic advantages of that waterway for our area and our province, and forward their report to the federal Minister of Transport. We formed a responsible committee of six riparian members and called a conference at Beloeil, in early December, when we invited an internationally known planner to address the conference on the advisability of the Richelieu waterway.

Richelieu Waterway
What happened? Our friends opposite sent us delegates to tell us: "Do not organize that conference with this great planner, you invited. Postpone it, because next December the federal Minister of Transport will address the chambers of commerce of Montreal and make an important statement about the Richelieu". Therefore, at their request, we cancelled our meeting, even though it was important, and waited for December. Then on December 7, 1960 we heard the Minister of Transport woefully confess that he had no intention of considering a problem that everybody wished would be looked into immediately.
Now, as we are discussing tonight a problem as important as the waterway, I say that we are tired to see that no minister nor Conservative member of parliament from Quebec is prepared to accept his responsibilities. We have had enough of ministers gadding about making political statements. We have had enough of seeing, as we do tonight, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, a nice chap, a wonderful chap, an extremely charming and courteous fellow, sitting here in silence and making his statements only outside the house.
When the time comes to speak in the house he stands there, candidly grinning at us and then he merely deputizes the inevitable member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm who dips both his feet into the river.

speechtext: Twenty two years of silence, only to talk nonsense in the opposition.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext: It did not take you that long.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, I would like to repeat this: the Minister of Transport told us that the Richelieu waterway would not be economically feasible. I asked him here a few days ago what he based his statement on. He replied that it was based on reports from his department's economists and engineers. I put on the order paper a motion for return, asking him to table the reports on which he based his statement that the waterway would not be economically feasible. The Minister of Transport replied that he would like me to withdraw the motion as he could not give an answer, because, as he said, the matter came under several departments.
Well, I would say tonight that it is time that the minister take his responsibilities and say here or elsewhere why he does not wish to encourage the study of the Richelieu waterway.
Many distinguished engineers, commissions of enquiry, renowned persons in the United
[Mr. Dupuis .1
States, all have admitted that the project was sound. They based their-

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext:
Don't kill the motion.
(Text):
If hon. members did not take our places when we are talking about Quebec matters, and if they did not waste our time I would have sufficient time to conclude my remarks in order to take a vote.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, the American engineers and the governor of Vermont are in favour of the Richelieu waterway.
The United States government is voting important sums of money to have army engineers undertake studies in that connection and, meanwhile, on this side of the border, our government is doing absolutely nothing in this field.
Following the statements made by my friends from Richelieu-Vercheres and Laurier, I repeat that the Richelieu waterway would shorten the distance between Montreal and New York from 1,800 miles to 400 miles.
The Richelieu waterway would also attract all transport vessels of low tonnage, and thus would clear the St. Lawrence seaway.
Manufacturers and industrialists would find it less costly to transport their merchandises through the Richelieu waterway, precisely on account of the greatly reduced distance.
Mr. Speaker, in our area of St. Jean-Iber-ville-Napierville, of Brome-Missisquoi-and I am wondering where is the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi-possibly the Richelieu waterway project is not a matter of interest to him-in our area of Chambly-Rouville, Ri-chelieu-Vercheres, Longueuil, Chateauguay-Laprairie, all people have their eyes set on this House of Commons. Tomorrow, they will read the papers and say: What did Mr. Balcer have to say? Nothing. What did the member for Chambly-Rouville say? Nothing. What did the member for Longueuil say? Nothing. What did the member for Brome-Missisquoi say? Nothing. What did the member for Chateau-guay-Huntingdon-Laprairie say? Nothing. Who represented Conservative aspirations in the House of Commons? The inevitable member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon).
Well, Mr. Speaker, the people of the province of Quebec will be in a position to see the difference between a Liberal team and a Conservative one.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext: What did the hon. member for Laurier do when he was minister of transport?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, would you
please call the member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm to order?
And now, Mr. Speaker, here is what Mr. Bennett said, on June 24, 1930, as recorded in the London Free Press of the same date:
If we come to power, we will undertake and complete the St. Lawrence seaway.
He came to power and he did nothing. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) came into our area. He told us: I came here to admire the fine scenery of the Richelieu. He went into lower Quebec and did nothing
Mr. Speaker, there are three minutes left before the house adjourns. If our friends are sincere, I shall resume my seat and ask them to vote in favour of the Richelieu waterway project.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY PROPOSED EXTENSION TO NEW YORK VIA RICHELIEU RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we heard the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) state that government members should stir up the people of the Richelieu area about the opportunity of developing a waterway. It seems to me, in view of his behaviour, that we have succeeded in stirring up the hon. member for Laurier.
If I had any advice to give to the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis), I would tell him that it is not by indulging in buffoonery or talking as he did tonight that we will bring the government to consider the opportunity of constructing the Richelieu cut-off.
The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) gave a rather complete account of the situation. However I believe that he is putting the cart before the horse when he suggests the establishment of a board of engineers to study the matter. I believe it would be more realistic to establish a commission made up of representatives of manufacturing organizations, labour unions, shipping interests, railways, as well as of industrialists and economists, to study the opportunity of developing such a project.
Business of the House
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I know much more about existing unused canals than about future ones. When it is a matter of coming to a decision on the construction of such an important waterway, requiring a very large investment, it should not be taken without due consideration. A study made on the spot by engineers would not show whether the project is economically feasible not only for the Quebec region but for the country as a whole.

INDENTURED APPRENTICES
speechtext:
1.	Are indentured apprentices included in schedule M of the federal Vocational Training Act?
2.	If not, has the government taken any steps to make indentured apprentices eligible to collect unemployment insurance benefits during their necessary training period in technical institutes?
3.	Have representations been received from any group requesting that indentured apprentices be permitted to draw unemployment insurance benefits during their training period in technical institutes?
4.	If so, from whom have such representations been received, and what reply was made?
Answer by: Hon. Michael Siarr (Minister of
Labour):
1.	No. The training for indentured apprentices is provided under a special federal-provincial apprenticeship training agreement.
2.	Yes. If an apprentice is unemployed and eligible for U.I.C. benefits before entering
his regular training period in a training centre he may continue to draw these benefits.
3.	Yes.
4.	The minister of labour for Saskatchewan, Hon. C. C. Williams. In reply he was informed that this matter was under consideration, and as soon as a final decision was reached by the unemployment insurance commission, he would be advised.
